---
title: "Pressure, action steps and possession outcomes"
---

PRESS studies pressure through possession fragility: defenders remove time and space from the carrier and restrict usable passing options, making ball retention harder. A backwards action alone does not establish pressure. The core estimate combines local action risks under an average policy conditioned on the current state; it does not estimate an individual player's personal policy or a causal effect of a specific defender. **design choice**

## Three separate units

| Unit | Meaning in PRESS |
|---|---|
| Observation frame | The tracking snapshot at which state and local action risks are evaluated. Any usable frame can be queried. |
| Canonical action step | A decision between a pass, evaluated through its execution, and a drive, evaluated over the configured horizon (currently one second by default). |
| Retrospective sequence | Selected evaluations along an observed team possession; completed passes continue the team sequence. |

The local hazard is a forward next-step estimate even when computed on a recorded match. The possession difficulty view retrospectively summarizes that estimate along the observed sequence. Arbitrary-frame access does not turn every tracking row into a new action step. An action-based hazard is dimensionless, not a per-second rate. **model scope**

## What the Fernandez framework specifies

The extended framework [@fernandez2021] uses pass, shot and drive actions, with a drive defined as one second of ball retention and its destination extrapolated at constant velocity. Its training examples combine annotated actions and tracking snapshots. Pass/drive success labels describe immediate execution; continuation models have a different reward. The extended paper sets that reward from the next goal, with zero assigned when it is more than 15 seconds away. EPV can then be queried frame by frame. See sections 5.2 and 6.1–6.2 of the [available preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2011.09426). The 2019 conference paper also uses one-second drives in its applications [@fernandez2019].

The [published 2021 version](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10994-021-05989-6), section 5.2, explicitly splits drives longer than one second into one-second drives. The [2019 paper](https://www.lukebornn.com/papers/fernandez_sloan_2019.pdf), section 6, samples its decision-analysis display every quarter-second while allowing every-frame evaluation. Prediction horizon and display sampling are separate. The reviewed passages do not specify a complete extraction algorithm for final partial windows or coincident boundaries. PRESS's corresponding rules remain project conventions. **processing boundary**

The accepted v2 policy keeps canonical one-second blocks anchored to the individual start and all failures, including short ones. Short non-loss tails contribute censored exposure to drive-rate estimation, without entering action selection. Passes remain at release; previous action is the start type before a full second of control and drive thereafter. Shot/foul/clearance preserve preceding drives and add evaluation snapshots. Forty zero-frame failures are retained with an explicit first-0.1-second timing-bin assumption. These are project conventions, not rules attributed to Fernández. **design choice**

A non-loss exposure contributes survival to its observed duration; failure contributes the probability of its frame-time interval. Predictions retain the canonical one-second horizon. Pass/shot stopping can be informative, so this likelihood does not automatically establish a causal risk under continued carrying or calibration under a natural action policy. Those questions remain for the benchmark. **model scope**

## Frame inference and retrospective aggregation

`compute_frame` resolves state/context independently of `get_checkpoints`. `compute_possession` uses canonical starts plus separately marked additional snapshots by default, or explicit `frame_ids`. Set `include_snapshots=False` to keep only canonical rows. Event annotation, action horizon and observation sampling are different contracts. **design choice**

For selected hazards, the package computes difficulty increments $D_k=-\log(1-h_k)$ and the product $S_K=\prod_k(1-h_k)$. The output is a retrospective path summary. A survival interpretation requires the rows to represent successive, nonoverlapping canonical risk steps, with consistent conditioning and terminal events; a list of arbitrary frame queries alone does not establish this. Dense overlapping one-second forecasts must not be treated as independent consecutive steps. The current selection, including short final intervals and pass boundaries, still requires benchmark review. **model scope**

## Why xLoss is an extra

The core task is to describe exposure, choices and execution under pressure. A continuation model can additionally predict whether the current individual's possession ends negatively. Successful passes terminate that individual's sequence but continue the team's sequence. These two endpoints must remain distinct. **design choice**

The [residual-risk vignette](vignettes/05a_residual_risk/05a_residual_risk.ipynb) documents the verified RR74 conditional terminal model and composes their loss probability with the local branches. It is optional and is not called by `PRESS.compute_frame` or `compute_possession`. Its target is the project's individual-possession terminal label, not an assertion that it reproduces SkillCorner's proprietary xLoss.

The optional residual training cohort uses successful full one-second canonical drives only, with features at drive start and a recorded completion frame. Clearance is final individual loss for this extra, while preceding control remains successful for drive execution. Short tails and shot-ending possessions are outside the residual cohort; RR74 evaluates this convention; the verified full-data deployment refit75 is installed separately from those OOF predictions.
